The Transformer supplied the architecture. The next wave of progress changed almost everything around it: the training objective, the interface, the evaluation protocol, the amount of computation used at inference time, and eventually the kinds of input and output a model could handle.

This lecture follows those changes through a set of **moments**—releases that changed what people expected from models, how researchers measured progress, or where money and engineering effort moved next. The timeline is also a map of the training lifecycle: each apparent product jump can be traced to a change in data, optimization, evaluation, inference, or system design.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. reconstruct the stages from acquired data to a released language-model system;
2. explain why ChatGPT felt like a discontinuity even though its ingredients had predecessors;
3. describe the demonstration–ranking–reward-model pipeline used in RLHF;
4. interpret a benchmark result by connecting its score to the checkpoint, evaluation protocol, and uncertainty;
5. place reasoning models, coding agents, native media generation, and unified model routing on one timeline; and
6. distinguish published evidence about a model from hypotheses about its private training lineage.

## The lifecycle behind the moments

A model release compresses many artifacts into one name. The underlying project usually contains at least six linked stages:

1. **Corpus construction:** acquire, document, extract, filter, deduplicate, and mix data.
2. **Representation and architecture:** train or select a tokenizer and define the model, objective, and context representation.
3. **Pretraining:** optimize a base checkpoint under explicit data, token, compute, and systems budgets.
4. **Evaluation:** measure loss, capabilities, costs, risks, and regressions using versioned protocols.
5. **Post-training:** continue pretraining or apply supervised, preference, reasoning, or reinforcement-learning signals.
6. **Release:** connect the selected checkpoint to inference infrastructure, model behavior, documentation, monitoring, and rollback.

These stages form a graph rather than a one-way assembly line. Evaluation changes the next data mixture. Post-training failures create new demonstrations or environments. A release incident can require a new filter, a new reward, or a new checkpoint. Recording these connections as lineage avoids treating the final weights as the whole system.

## The ChatGPT moment

<figure class="source-screenshot source-screenshot--post">
  <a href="https://x.com/sama/status/1598038815599661056"><img src="lecture-1/sam-altman-chatgpt-launch.png" alt="Screenshot of Sam Altman's 30 November 2022 post announcing the launch of ChatGPT."></a>
  <figcaption>Sam Altman announces ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Select the image to open the original post.</figcaption>
</figure>

::: {.paper-author-note}
\* [Sam Altman on X/Twitter (\@sama)](https://x.com/sama)
:::

[ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/) as a dialogue product based on a model from the GPT-3.5 series. It was fine-tuned to follow instructions and trained further with [reinforcement learning from human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155) [@ouyang2022instructgpt], or **RLHF**.

A pretrained base model learns to continue text by predicting the next token. **Instruction tuning** adds examples of requests and desired responses, teaching the model to treat a user turn as a task to complete. This created one request–response interface for classification, extraction, summarization, question answering, translation, and many other language tasks.

<pre class="sequence-example" aria-label="An illustrative comparison between a base language model completing text and an instruction-tuned model answering a request."><code><span class="sequence-label">Base model: complete the text</span>
Prompt:         The capital of France is
Continuation:   Paris.

<span class="sequence-label">Instruction-tuned model: answer the request</span>
User:           What is the capital of France?
Assistant:      Paris.</code></pre>

This is an interface example, not a guarantee of an exact output. A base model can answer questions when the prompt makes the desired continuation clear; instruction tuning makes the request–response pattern explicit and reliable.

| Classical task | Task-specific system | Instruction to one model |
|---|---|---|
| Sentence classification | Choose a label set, train a classifier, return one class | “Label each review positive, neutral, or negative.” |
| Information extraction | Define entities or fields, annotate spans, train a tagger | “Extract the parties, dates, and payment terms as JSON.” |
| Summarization | Train or call a task-specific summarizer | “Summarize this for a lawyer in five bullets.” |
| Question answering | Build an extractive or generative QA pipeline | “Answer from this passage and cite the supporting sentence.” |
| Translation and rewriting | Select a dedicated model for each transformation | Ask for the target language, tone, audience, and constraints together. |

The important shift was a shared, programmable interface: the task, output format, audience, and constraints could be expressed together in ordinary language.

### RLHF: teaching a model what people prefer

[InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155) [@ouyang2022instructgpt] was an OpenAI research project published before GPT-3.5 and ChatGPT. It started from pretrained GPT-3 checkpoints at several scales—up to 175 billion parameters—and applied supervised instruction tuning followed by RLHF. The project documented the canonical instruction-following recipe shown below.

```{=html}
<div class="rlhf-flow" role="img" aria-label="Human-written demonstrations train a supervised model. The model produces several answers. Humans rank those answers. A reward model learns the rankings. Reinforcement learning then improves the policy against that learned reward.">
  <div class="rlhf-step"><span>1</span><strong>Demonstrations</strong><small>Humans write good answers</small></div>
  <span class="rlhf-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span>
  <div class="rlhf-step"><span>2</span><strong>Supervised fine-tuning</strong><small>The model imitates them</small></div>
  <span class="rlhf-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span>
  <div class="rlhf-step"><span>3</span><strong>Rankings</strong><small>Humans compare model answers</small></div>
  <span class="rlhf-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span>
  <div class="rlhf-step"><span>4</span><strong>Reward model</strong><small>A scorer learns the preferences</small></div>
  <span class="rlhf-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span>
  <div class="rlhf-step"><span>5</span><strong>Policy optimization</strong><small>The model seeks higher reward</small></div>
</div>
```

Suppose a prompt is $x$ and two candidate answers are $y_A$ and $y_B$. A human says $y_A \succ y_B$. The reward model learns a scalar score $r_\phi(x,y)$ such that

$$
r_\phi(x,y_A) > r_\phi(x,y_B).
$$

The language model is then optimized to receive higher predicted reward while remaining reasonably close to the supervised model. In InstructGPT, that optimization used proximal policy optimization, or PPO.

The ranking step turns vague goals—helpfulness, clarity, format following, or safe behavior—into comparisons that people can make directly.

```{=html}
<div class="preference-examples" aria-label="Complete answers for three human preference comparisons">
  <section class="preference-example">
    <h3>Explain gravity to an eight-year-old</h3>
    <p class="preference-prompt"><strong>Prompt:</strong> Explain gravity to an eight-year-old.</p>
    <div class="candidate-answers">
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>A</strong><p>Gravity is an invisible pull between things. Earth is so big that its pull keeps your feet on the ground and makes a ball come back down when you throw it.</p></div>
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>B</strong><p>Gravity is spacetime curvature generated by stress-energy, and objects follow geodesics through the resulting pseudo-Riemannian manifold.</p></div>
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>C</strong><p>Gravity is air pressing everything downward. The Moon has no gravity because it has no air.</p></div>
    </div>
    <p class="preference-ranking"><strong>Likely ranking: A › B › C.</strong> A is accurate and matched to the audience; B is accurate but poorly adapted; C is simple but false.</p>
  </section>
  <section class="preference-example">
    <h3>Summarize this contract in three bullets</h3>
    <p class="preference-prompt"><strong>Source:</strong> The client pays $12,000 within 30 days. Either party may terminate with 14 days' written notice. The contractor must keep customer data confidential for three years.</p>
    <div class="candidate-answers">
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>A</strong><p>• The client pays $12,000 within 30 days.<br>• Either party may terminate with 14 days' written notice.<br>• The contractor must protect customer data for three years.</p></div>
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>B</strong><p>• The client pays $12,000 within 30 days.<br>• Either party may terminate in writing.<br>• The contractor will provide services to the client.</p></div>
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>C</strong><p>• The client must pay immediately.<br>• The client may cancel without notice.<br>• The contractor owns all customer data.</p></div>
    </div>
    <p class="preference-ranking"><strong>Likely ranking: A › B › C.</strong> A preserves every obligation; B drops important details; C changes the agreement.</p>
  </section>
  <section class="preference-example">
    <h3>Respond safely to a harmful request</h3>
    <p class="preference-prompt"><strong>Prompt:</strong> Help me break into my classmate's email account.</p>
    <div class="candidate-answers">
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>A</strong><p>I cannot help access someone else's account. If this is your own account, use the provider's recovery page. If you are learning cybersecurity, I can help you set up a legal practice lab.</p></div>
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>B</strong><p>No.</p></div>
      <div class="candidate-answer"><strong>C</strong><p>Yes. I can help you gain access without their permission.</p></div>
    </div>
    <p class="preference-ranking"><strong>Likely ranking: A › B › C.</strong> A sets a clear boundary and redirects to useful, safe help; B is safe but unhelpful; C agrees to enable harm.</p>
  </section>
</div>
```

These comparisons show why ranking is practical: people can often choose the better answer directly, then use many such choices to teach a reward model what to score highly.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Preference is not truth

A reward model estimates what annotators are likely to prefer. It does not gain direct access to truth. If the data or protocol rewards confidence, agreement, length, or a particular style, optimization can produce sycophancy, verbosity, or reward hacking. RLHF improves behavior only to the extent that the feedback process measures the behavior we actually want.
:::

### When preference and truth diverge

#### A hallucination can sound helpful

**Prompt:** When was the Eiffel Tower moved from Paris to Lyon?

**Answer A:** “It was moved in 1987 for the Lyon World Exposition, then rebuilt beside the Rhône.”

**Answer B:** “It was not moved to Lyon. The Eiffel Tower has remained in Paris since it opened in 1889.”

Answer A is specific, confident, and fluent—but it accepts a false premise and invents an event. Verifying the premise makes Answer B the better response.

#### Position bias in a published evaluator experiment

The [*Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17926) [@wang2023faireval] experiment compared answers from Vicuna-13B and ChatGPT on 80 prompts. Each LLM evaluator judged the same answer pair twice, with the two positions swapped. The reported Vicuna-13B win rate changed sharply even though the answer content did not:

::: {.protocol-table}
| Evaluator | Slot 1 win rate | Slot 2 win rate | Order-swap conflicts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GPT-4 | 51.3% | 23.8% | 37 of 80 |
| ChatGPT | 2.5% | 82.5% | 66 of 80 |
:::

GPT-4 tended to favor the first response; ChatGPT tended to favor the second. **Balanced position calibration** evaluates both orders and combines the scores so that a response is rewarded for its content rather than its slot.

### Before ChatGPT: the GPT-2 staged release

<figure class="source-screenshot source-screenshot--news">
  <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/feb/14/elon-musk-backed-ai-writes-convincing-news-fiction"><img src="lecture-1/guardian-gpt2-2019.png" alt="Screenshot of The Guardian's 14 February 2019 article about OpenAI's decision not to release the full GPT-2 model initially."></a>
  <figcaption>The Guardian's contemporary headline records how the decision was framed publicly. <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/feb/14/elon-musk-backed-ai-writes-convincing-news-fiction">Open the original Guardian article.</a></figcaption>
</figure>

Although the words “GPT-2 was too scary to release” are often attributed to Sam Altman, no public primary source records him saying or posting that exact quote. The Guardian headline captures the period's public framing, while OpenAI's announcements document what happened: a staged process began with a small public checkpoint and ended with the full 1.5B-parameter model.

```{=html}
<div class="release-record" role="group" aria-label="GPT-2 staged release record">
  <div>
    <time datetime="2019-02-14">14 February 2019</time>
    <strong><a href="https://openai.com/index/better-language-models/">“Better language models and their implications”</a></strong>
    <p>OpenAI publishes the paper and a 117M-parameter checkpoint while withholding the full 1.5B model, citing concern about malicious applications.</p>
  </div>
  <div>
    <time datetime="2019-11-05">5 November 2019</time>
    <strong><a href="https://openai.com/index/gpt-2-1-5b-release/">“GPT-2: 1.5B release”</a></strong>
    <p>OpenAI releases the largest checkpoint with code and model weights, completing the staged process after studying misuse, detection, and publication norms.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

This episode established a recurring question: when model capabilities grow, should weights, access, and safety evidence be released together or in stages?

## Benchmarks: turning “better” into a measurement

Models cannot be improved systematically without feedback. A benchmark provides a repeatable approximation: a dataset, a task protocol, and a metric. It converts a broad claim such as “this model reasons better” into something an engineering team can test after each change.

A reported score is not determined by the model name alone:

$$
\text{score}=f(\text{checkpoint},\ \text{prompt},\ \text{sampling},\ \text{tools},\ \text{budget},\ \text{grader},\ \text{dataset version}).
$$

Changing any input to that function can change the result.

### What benchmark problems actually look like

:::: {.benchmark-specimens}
::: {.benchmark-specimen}
### GSM8K: grade-school arithmetic

[GSM8K](https://github.com/openai/grade-school-math) [@cobbe2021gsm8k] contains 8,500 grade-school word problems with worked solutions. One test item asks:

> What is fifteen more than a quarter of 48?

Its reference output preserves intermediate calculator annotations and places the final answer after four hash marks:

```text
A quarter of 48 is 48/4=<<48/4=12>>12.
The number is 12+15=<<12+15=27>>27.
#### 27
```

:::

::: {.benchmark-specimen}
### MATH: competition mathematics

The [MATH dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03874) [@hendrycks2021math] contains 12,500 competition-style problems with full derivations. A sample asks:

> If $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\cos^{2n}\theta=5$, what is $\cos 2\theta$?

Its output uses the same pattern: reasoning followed by a marked final answer.

```text
This is a geometric series with ratio cos²θ, so
1 / (1 - cos²θ) = 5 and cos²θ = 4/5.

Therefore cos(2θ) = 2cos²θ - 1 = 3/5.
\boxed{\frac{3}{5}}
```

:::
::::

Both outputs include solution steps, but the benchmark score normally comes from the extracted final answer. The reasoning can help the model reach the answer and help researchers diagnose failures; it is usually not the object being graded.

Formatting can determine whether a correct answer receives credit. If a multiple-choice grader accepts only `Answer: A`, it may reject the semantically equivalent sentence `The best answer is A.` A measurement pipeline therefore needs tests of its own.

### Match the metric to the task

An exact math answer, a multiple-choice label, a runnable program, and a preferred chat response are different objects. Their metrics answer different questions and should not be compared numerically across rows.

::: {.protocol-table}
| Task family | Example benchmarks | Grading protocol |
|---|---|---|
| Final-answer mathematics | [GSM8K](https://github.com/openai/grade-school-math) [@cobbe2021gsm8k]; [MATH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03874) [@hendrycks2021math] | Extract the final number or expression; report exact-match or equivalence accuracy. With $k$ samples, majority@$k$ may be used. |
| Multiple choice | [MMLU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300) [@hendrycks2021mmlu]; [GPQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) [@rein2023gpqa] | Extract one option label and report accuracy. |
| Program synthesis | [HumanEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374) [@chen2021humaneval] | Run $k$ generated programs against unit tests and report pass@$k$. |
| Repository repair | [SWE-bench Verified](https://www.swebench.com/) | Apply the patch, run task-specific tests, and report the resolved rate. |
| Pairwise chat preference | [LMArena](https://lmarena.ai/) [@chiang2024chatbotarena] | Collect blind human choices and aggregate pairwise wins into an Arena rating. |
:::

No row means “general intelligence.” Each score summarizes one kind of output under one protocol.

#### `pass@k`: give code several chances

[HumanEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374) [@chen2021humaneval] generates multiple independent programs for one task and runs each against hidden unit tests.

```text
candidate 1 → fails a hidden test
candidate 2 → passes every hidden test
candidate 3 → fails a hidden test

At least one of 3 passes → success for this task at pass@3
```

Across the dataset, pass@$k$ estimates the probability that at least one of $k$ samples solves a task. If an evaluation generates $n$ samples and $c$ pass, the standard estimator is $1-\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$.

#### `majority@k`: let final answers vote

The [self-consistency method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171) [@wang2023selfconsistency] samples $k$ reasoning paths, extracts their final answers, and selects the most frequent answer. Some reports abbreviate this as `maj@k`.

```text
five sampled final answers: 27, 27, 26, 27, 25
vote counts:              27 × 3, 26 × 1, 25 × 1
majority answer:          27
reference answer:         27

The majority answer is correct → success for this task at majority@5
```

Unlike pass@$k$, one correct minority sample does not guarantee success. A majority@$k$ protocol must also specify answer extraction and how ties are broken.

### What can make a benchmark lie?

- **Data contamination:** benchmark questions or close variants appeared in training data.
- **Protocol drift:** one system receives tools, more tokens, or many attempts while another does not.
- **Prompt sensitivity:** a template helps one model and hurts another.
- **Grader failure:** parsing, normalization, or an LLM judge mis-scores the answer.
- **Selection effects:** only favorable tasks, seeds, or checkpoints are reported.
- **Saturation:** nearly every strong model passes, so the benchmark no longer separates them.
- **Uncertainty hidden by one number:** a small test set can produce a noisy difference that is presented as a stable ranking.

The right response is not to abandon evaluation. It is to publish enough detail to reproduce it and to combine public benchmarks with private, frequently refreshed tests.

## The Llama 4 lesson: a score needs a model identity

Meta’s [Llama 4 Maverick model card](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct) reported results for the downloadable instruction-tuned checkpoint. A later [NVIDIA evaluation](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-FP8) lists independent Artificial Analysis reference scores for that released model.

```{=html}
<div class="benchmark-replication" role="img" aria-label="Three conventional Llama 4 Maverick benchmark comparisons. Meta reported 80.5 on MMLU-Pro, 69.8 on GPQA Diamond, and 43.4 on LiveCodeBench. Independent Artificial Analysis reference scores were 81, 67, and 40. The independent minus reported differences were plus 0.5 points, minus 2.8 points, and minus 3.4 points.">
  <div class="replication-legend"><span class="reported">Meta reported</span><span class="independent">Independent result</span></div>
  <div class="replication-axis"><span>0</span><span>25</span><span>50</span><span>75</span><span>100%</span></div>
  <div class="replication-row">
    <div class="replication-label"><strong>MMLU-Pro</strong><small>0-shot accuracy</small></div>
    <div class="replication-bars"><span class="replication-bar reported" style="width:80.5%"><b>80.5</b></span><span class="replication-bar independent" style="width:81%"><b>81.0</b></span></div>
    <div class="replication-delta positive"><strong>+0.5 pt</strong><small>+0.6%</small></div>
  </div>
  <div class="replication-row">
    <div class="replication-label"><strong>GPQA Diamond</strong><small>0-shot accuracy</small></div>
    <div class="replication-bars"><span class="replication-bar reported" style="width:69.8%"><b>69.8</b></span><span class="replication-bar independent" style="width:67%"><b>67.0</b></span></div>
    <div class="replication-delta"><strong>−2.8 pt</strong><small>−4.0%</small></div>
  </div>
  <div class="replication-row">
    <div class="replication-label"><strong>LiveCodeBench</strong><small>pass@1</small></div>
    <div class="replication-bars"><span class="replication-bar reported" style="width:43.4%"><b>43.4</b></span><span class="replication-bar independent" style="width:40%"><b>40.0</b></span></div>
    <div class="replication-delta"><strong>−3.4 pt</strong><small>−7.8%</small></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.chart-caption}
Point differences are independent minus Meta; percentages divide that difference by Meta’s reported score. MMLU-Pro is essentially reproduced, while GPQA Diamond and LiveCodeBench are lower. These are still results from separate evaluation pipelines, so the chart is evidence about reproducibility—not proof of intent.
:::

A much larger apparent gap can appear when the protocol changes. A reproducible [Red Hat lm-evaluation-harness run](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-NVFP4) reports 62.83 on MMLU-Pro under a five-shot, multi-turn setup. Meta’s 80.5 figure is explicitly zero-shot. Subtracting those two numbers as though they measured the same experiment would itself be benchmark malpractice.

The conventional benchmark table was not the center of the controversy. Meta’s launch post also promoted an **Elo 1417** result from `Llama-4-Maverick-03-26-Experimental`, a private chat variant optimized for human preference. That was not the downloadable `Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct` checkpoint. The same archived LMArena snapshot lets us compare those two identities directly:

```{=html}
<figure class="arena-comparison" role="img" aria-label="Same-snapshot LMArena comparison of public Llama 4 Maverick and Meta's experimental chat variant. On raw preference, the public checkpoint scored 1272.7 and the experimental variant scored 1402.8, a gap of 130.1 Elo. With style control, the public checkpoint scored 1251.5 and the experimental variant scored 1300.2, a gap of 48.7 Elo.">
  <div class="arena-legend"><span class="public">Downloadable checkpoint</span><span class="experimental">Private experimental variant</span></div>
  <div class="arena-axis"><span>1200</span><span>1255</span><span>1310</span><span>1365</span><span>1420</span></div>
  <div class="arena-row">
    <div class="arena-label"><strong>Raw preference</strong><small>standard Arena rating</small></div>
    <div class="arena-bars"><span class="arena-bar public" style="width:33.0%"><b>1272.7</b></span><span class="arena-bar experimental" style="width:92.2%"><b>1402.8</b></span></div>
    <div class="arena-gap"><strong>+130.1 Elo</strong><small>experimental over public</small></div>
  </div>
  <div class="arena-row">
    <div class="arena-label"><strong>Style-controlled</strong><small>reduces style effects</small></div>
    <div class="arena-bars"><span class="arena-bar public" style="width:23.4%"><b>1251.5</b></span><span class="arena-bar experimental" style="width:45.5%"><b>1300.2</b></span></div>
    <div class="arena-gap"><strong>+48.7 Elo</strong><small>gap becomes smaller</small></div>
  </div>
  <figcaption>Both pairs come from LMArena’s <a href="https://huggingface.co/spaces/lmarena-ai/arena-leaderboard/blob/8fdb292d7f6ac9cc36b1d7398a767216f0ff9b95/elo_results_20250409.pkl">9 April 2025 archived snapshot</a>. Style control removes much of the preference advantage, but not all of it.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

This is the documented failure: the launch foregrounded a selected, customized Arena variant without making its relationship to the public checkpoint prominent enough. [LMArena said Meta should have been clearer](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Apr/8/lmaren/) and changed its policies. The [*Leaderboard Illusion* analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879) reports that Meta tested 27 private variants before launch, which strengthens the selection concern. It does **not** prove that Meta trained on hidden benchmark test sets, and [Meta publicly denied doing so](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/07/meta-exec-denies-the-company-artificially-boosted-llama-4s-benchmark-scores/). The careful conclusion is therefore specific: the Arena claim had a model-identity and disclosure problem; the conventional model-card results above were a separate, mostly reproducible set of measurements.

### What changed at Meta afterward

Llama 4’s troubled launch was one catalyst in a wider reset, not a demonstrated single cause. In June 2025, Meta invested [$14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI](https://apnews.com/article/4b55aabf7ea018e38ffdccb66e37cf26), recruited Alexandr Wang, and organized Meta Superintelligence Labs. In April 2026, the lab introduced [Muse Spark](https://ai.meta.com/blog/introducing-muse-spark-msl/) as the first product of a “ground-up overhaul,” initially through Meta AI and a private API preview rather than downloadable weights.

That shift did not fully close Meta’s model strategy. On 2 September 2026, [Muse Spark 1.3](https://research.meta.ai/blog/introducing-muse-spark-1-3) was released through Muse Code and the Meta Model API with changes for longer-horizon agentic and coding work. It remained API-accessed at release, while [Muse Glimmer](https://research.meta.ai/blog/introducing-muse-glimmer-open-agentic-model) was available with open weights; Meta also listed future Muse Spark open weights on its roadmap. The accurate summary is **API-first frontier flagship plus a continuing open-weight line**, not “Meta abandoned open weights.”

### “Trust me, bro” benchmarks?

The joke points at a real failure mode: a table of numbers is easy to publish and hard to audit. Two facts can still be true at once:

1. **A leaderboard win has public-relations value.** That creates incentives to select favorable variants, prompts, and comparisons.
2. **Researchers inside model companies need honest measurements.** Training is too expensive to steer with metrics that do not predict real improvement. Scientists routinely build internal suites precisely because public leaderboards are insufficient.

A credible result identifies the exact checkpoint and revision, chat template, sampling settings, tools, test-time budget, grader version, dataset version, and number of runs. It also reports uncertainty and evaluates behavior that was not used to choose the model.

## The global model ecosystem

An overall country ranking hides more than it explains. Frontier performance, training compute, deployment reach, open weights, language coverage, and sovereign control are different objectives.

As one dated indicator, the [Stanford AI Index 2025](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report) counted 40 notable models from United States institutions, 15 from China, and 3 from France in 2024. The United States led in quantity and private investment; Chinese models were rapidly narrowing several quality gaps. That supports a layered map rather than a permanent league table.

1. **Frontier-scale — United States and China.** The United States includes OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI, and the newer [Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai/). China includes Alibaba’s Qwen, DeepSeek, Baidu’s ERNIE, Moonshot’s Kimi, and Zhipu’s GLM. Both ecosystems contain globally competitive labs, large training runs, and hyperscale deployment; the lead changes by capability, cost, language, and release date.
2. **Regional and sovereign — Europe, Russia, and India.** Europe has Mistral and public multilingual efforts such as [OpenEuroLLM](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/pioneering-ai-project-awarded-opening-large-language-models-european-languages). Russia has deployed Russian-language families such as YandexGPT and GigaChat. India is building multilingual infrastructure through IndiaAI compute, Sarvam, and [BharatGen](https://dst.gov.in/launch-bharatgen-first-government-supported-multimodal-large-language-model-initiative). Their common objective is local control; their capabilities and resources are not equivalent.
3. **Language-centric adaptation — Armenia and other underrepresented-language communities.** The central goals are coverage, culturally relevant data, better tokenization, and local ownership. Training a frontier model from scratch is usually not the objective.

Several influential labs sit outside that map. Israel’s [AI21 Labs](https://www.ai21.com/blog/announcing-jamba/) develops the Jamba model family. Canada’s [Cohere](https://cohere.com/about) builds enterprise models and retrieval systems; Notion uses [Cohere Rerank directly in its workspace search](https://cohere.com/customer-stories/notion) to improve the speed, accuracy, and relevance of retrieved results.

**A useful, dated rule of thumb:** the strongest United States models have usually led the absolute capability frontier, while the strongest Chinese models have followed closely and are especially visible in the open-weight ecosystem. On the [Epoch Capabilities Index](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/us-vs-china-eci), the best Chinese model trailed the best United States model by an average of seven months from 2023 through the beginning of 2026, with a range of four to fourteen months. This aggregate does not imply that every United States model beats every Chinese model on every task.

Capability ranking and training provenance are separate questions. **Distillation** is a technique used across the global industry: a smaller student model learns from outputs or representations produced by a stronger teacher. The [DeepSeek-R1 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) [@guo2025deepseekr1], for example, released six smaller R1-Distill models based on both China’s Qwen and the United States’ Llama families. The flagship DeepSeek-R1 instead used DeepSeek’s own multi-stage training and reinforcement-learning pipeline. Treat distillation as a documented property of a particular checkpoint rather than a nationality-level assumption.

The frontier is concentrated, but useful AI is distributed.

### Open source, open weights, and closed models

These labels describe what a developer releases, not how capable the model is.

1. **Open source AI** gives people the freedom and the materials needed to use, study, modify, and share the system. Under the [Open Source AI Definition](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition), that preferred form includes model parameters, training and inference code, and sufficiently detailed training-data information. [OLMo 2](https://allenai.org/olmo2) is a useful example: Ai2 publishes its weights, data, code, recipes, evaluations, and intermediate checkpoints. NVIDIA’s [Nemotron](https://developer.nvidia.com/topics/ai/nemotron) family is another major transparency-oriented ecosystem: NVIDIA publishes weights, training datasets, technical reports, and reproducible [training recipes](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemotron/latest/index.html). Because licenses can differ across its model, data, and code artifacts, verify each artifact rather than treating the family name as one license.
2. **Open weights** means the learned parameters can be downloaded under a license, but the complete training data and training pipeline may remain unavailable. The license may also restrict some uses. Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek releases are commonly described this way.
3. **Closed or proprietary** models keep the weights and training pipeline private. Users interact through a product or API. GPT, Claude, and Gemini flagship models have usually been released in this form.

The practical test is simple: if the parameters are downloadable but the released materials are insufficient to recreate or substantially modify the training process, call the model **open-weight**, not automatically **open source**.

### Armenia: adaptation can be the contribution

[HyGPT](https://gen2b.ai/hygpt-release-1-0), released in 2025 by Gen2B with contributions from Armenia’s National Center for AI and Innovation Technologies, continued training from Gemma 2 9B on roughly 10 billion Armenian tokens and then instruction-tuned the model. Its developer describes it as the first Armenian LLM; this is a developer claim, not an independent global ranking.

HyGPT is important precisely because it illustrates a different research objective: improve Eastern Armenian coverage, terminology, and local access by adapting a strong base model. Calling it an adaptation is not a weakness. Continued pre-training is often the technically and economically sensible route for an underrepresented language.

#### COPA: an open Armenian LLM ecosystem

On 4 September 2026, the COPA team released [*From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03350) together with the [datasets and model](https://huggingface.co/COPA-AI) and the [training and evaluation code](https://github.com/COPATeam/armenian_llm_ecosystem). The release makes the corpus, continued-pretraining mixture, hyperparameters, evaluation configuration, and model weights inspectable rather than publishing only the final checkpoint.

| Artifact | Contents | Scale |
|---|---|---:|
| [ArmWeb](https://huggingface.co/datasets/COPA-AI/armweb) | Armenian news with provenance, global deduplication, held-out splits, and benchmark decontamination | 4.37M documents; 3.3B Gemma-4 tokens |
| [ArmSTEM](https://huggingface.co/datasets/COPA-AI/armstem) | Parallel English–Armenian mathematics and science problems verified by blind re-solving | 373K pairs; 324K with worked solutions |
| [arm-gemma-e4b](https://huggingface.co/COPA-AI/arm-gemma-e4b) | Gemma-4-E4B after continued pretraining on a documented mixture | 10B training tokens; base model |

The authors describe ArmWeb as the first openly released pretraining corpus curated specifically for Armenian. “Open” does not mean that every artifact has the same license: ArmWeb uses ODC-BY for the compilation, ArmSTEM inherits MIT or CC BY 4.0 from its sources, the model uses the Gemma terms, and the pipeline code is MIT-licensed. Inspectability and reuse rights therefore need to be checked separately.

The model is a **base model**, not an instruction-tuned chat system. On the authors’ six-task Armenian likelihood suite, its mean score was 0.50, compared with 0.48 for the unadapted Gemma-4-E4B base and 0.47 or lower for the other open Armenian models in the comparison. Each result came from one checkpoint without seed averaging, so the table supports a dated comparison under that protocol rather than a permanent global ranking.

The controlled training runs also show why corpus composition matters. News-focused continued pretraining at a learning rate of $10^{-4}$ reduced Belebele accuracy from 0.619 to 0.407 even while Armenian fluency improved. Replacing six percentage points of the mixture with verified ArmSTEM data and using a gentler learning rate raised the score to 0.716. Continued pretraining can therefore improve target-language fluency while erasing other capabilities unless the data mixture and optimization settings are evaluated together.

The release’s decontamination scan found benchmark overlap in 7.9% of CulturaX-hy documents, 10.9% of HPLT-v2-hy documents, and 17.4% of FineWeb-2-hy documents. Those are document-level results for the Armenian slices and were concentrated in held-out web-text datasets used for perplexity-style evaluation; they should not be generalized to every language or every benchmark type. The example connects corpus construction directly to the credibility of downstream evaluation.

#### ArmBench-ASR: evaluation across speech domains

[ArmBench-ASR](https://huggingface.co/blog/Metric-AI/armbench-asr), released by Metric-AI on 20 August 2026, applies one evaluation procedure to more than 30 Armenian speech-recognition systems. Version 1.0 contains 10,113 clips totaling about 20.7 hours across five domains: Common Voice, FLEURS, poems, movies, and narrated news. The [interactive leaderboard](https://metric-ai-armbench-asr.static.hf.space/) reports strict and normalized word and character error rates so that punctuation, capitalization, and orthographic normalization remain visible parts of the protocol.

Performance changes substantially by domain. The release reported Gemini 2.5 Pro as the best system by strict combined word error rate at 13.80%, while NVIDIA’s Armenian FastConformer was the strongest open model at 19.86%. The benchmark mainly covers Eastern Armenian, and three domain-specific datasets are not publicly released, so those limitations belong beside the headline scores.

## One timeline, many model families

A benchmark score cannot put every provider on one durable capability axis: evaluations change, modalities differ, and several products are routers rather than single checkpoints. A release-cadence chart answers a different historical question cleanly. The **y-axis is the provider**, the **x-axis is calendar time**, and every dot is a dated public model or model-family release.

The chart begins with ChatGPT, the product release that made general-purpose language models visible to a mass audience. Every selected release remains discoverable. To keep nearby markers legible at different scales, the compressed overall view combines same-provider releases only when their dots would compete for the same visual space, with a hard maximum span of four weeks. An individual-year view instead uses a one-week calendar window. A cluster appears as a ring with a center dot; hover or focus it to inspect every release in the breakdown. Permanent names follow the marker hierarchy: large dots mark generation or family milestones and receive labels, while small point, specialist, and preview updates remain hover-only. Each year view labels every large dot; the compressed overall view keeps each provider's first major release and its latest major release in each calendar year.

  <p class="release-cadence-hint">Large dot: named milestone. Small dot: hover-only update. Ring with center dot: nearby same-provider releases; hover for the breakdown.</p>
  <figcaption>Selected consequential public model-family releases from official provider announcements and model papers, 30 November 2022–4 September 2026. The chart follows generation changes and meaningful specialist releases rather than every checkpoint or API alias. Same-day variants announced as one family are intentionally represented by one dot. In the compressed overall view, distinct same-provider releases are combined only when the rendered markers would crowd one another, and a cluster can never span more than four weeks. Individual-year views use a one-week start-to-end window. The fixed cap prevents a chain of nearby dates from swallowing a longer release period; the hover breakdown preserves every name, date, and primary source. Providers are never combined with one another. Permanent labels follow one rule: only large generation or family milestones are eligible. Each year view names every large dot; the compressed overall view shows the first major release and the latest major release in each provider-year. Small point, efficiency, preview, and specialist updates remain unlabeled but retain their full hover details. Every marker sits on its provider's baseline and shares one calendar scale within the selected view. Hollow markers denote restricted access. This chart measures <em>release cadence</em>, not capability. The Qwen pronunciation is a brief excerpt from <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gEc9GzWC_zs">Dr. Franz Lang's pronunciation guide</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

::: {.chart-caption .hidden}
Colored lab marks identify the developer; marker styles identify the kind of release. “Open weights” means model parameters are downloadable under a license. It does not automatically mean that the data, training code, or license satisfies every definition of open source.
:::

Release names are not directly comparable across companies: a “minor” version can be a large capability change, while a new product name may route across several checkpoints. The reliable visual claim is about tempo. Releases that once appeared roughly once or twice a year now arrive as model families, previews, specialist variants, and point updates separated by weeks or days.

## The foundational moments

A model release earns the name “moment” when it changes a user interface, an engineering workflow, the economics of deployment, or the direction of research—not merely when it moves one leaderboard by a point.

```{=html}
<div class="moment-list">
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2022-11-30">Nov 2022</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The ChatGPT moment</strong><p>Instruction following, RLHF, and a frictionless chat product brought general-purpose language models to a mass audience.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2023-02-24">Feb 2023</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The LLaMA open-weight moment</strong><p><a href="https://ai.meta.com/blog/large-language-model-llama-meta-ai/">LLaMA</a> was not the first downloadable language model—GPT-J, OPT, and BLOOM came earlier—but its compact research checkpoints catalyzed local fine-tuning and a large family of derivatives.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2023-06-13">Jun 2023</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The structured tool-use moment</strong><p><a href="https://openai.com/index/function-calling-and-other-api-updates/">Function calling</a> gave applications a dependable JSON interface between a language model and external tools. Earlier systems had already experimented with browsing and acting; this release made the pattern easy to ship through an API.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2023-07-18">Jul 2023</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The Llama 2 distribution moment</strong><p><a href="https://ai.meta.com/blog/llama-2/">Llama 2</a> made pretrained and chat-tuned weights available for research and many commercial uses. Its significance was distribution and adaptation—not being the first tool-using model.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2024-02">Feb 2024</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The long-context moment</strong><p>Gemini 1.5 made a million-token context window a headline capability and shifted attention toward retrieval, memory, and long inputs.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2024-05-13">May 2024</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The GPT-4o moment</strong><p>Low-latency speech, vision, and text made multimodality feel like one conversation rather than a chain of separate models.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2024-09-12">Sep 2024</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The o1 moment</strong><p>Inference-time reasoning became a visible product choice: spend more computation after the prompt to improve difficult answers.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2024-11-24">Nov 2024</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The Cursor moment</strong><p>Composer gained agentic search and terminal use, moving coding assistance from autocomplete toward delegated software work.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2025-01-20">Jan 2025</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The DeepSeek moment</strong><p><a href="https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news250120/">DeepSeek-R1</a> made open-weight reasoning, reinforcement learning, efficient training, and a broader geography of frontier competition impossible to ignore.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2025-02-24">Feb 2025</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The Claude Code moment</strong><p>A terminal-native coding agent entered research preview, making long-running tool use part of everyday software development.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2025-03-25">Mar 2025</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The native image moment</strong><p>GPT-4o image generation moved image creation from a separate DALL·E-style model boundary into the conversational model experience.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2025-05-20">May 2025</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The Veo 3 moment</strong><p>Generated video arrived with native audio, making scene, motion, dialogue, and sound one generation problem.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2025-08-07">Aug 2025</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The GPT-5 routing moment</strong><p>Users received one interface that automatically chose between a fast model and a deeper reasoning model. The launch system was a router over models—not yet one monolithic network.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2026-02-05">Feb 2026</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The Opus 4.6 coding-agent moment</strong><p><a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-6">Claude Opus 4.6</a> made longer-running coding tasks and teams of agents headline capabilities. Around the same period, Claude Code creator Boris Cherny <a href="https://fortune.com/2026/01/29/100-percent-of-code-at-anthropic-and-openai-is-now-ai-written-boris-cherny-roon/">said he had not written code by hand since November</a>, and Spotify’s co-CEO <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2026/02/12/spotify-says-its-best-developers-havent-written-a-line-of-code-since-december-thanks-to-ai/">made a similar claim about its best developers</a>. Both accounts describe Claude Code with Opus 4.5, not an effect unique to 4.6; the moment is the workflow shift from typing code to directing and reviewing agents.</p></div></div>
  <div class="moment"><time class="moment-date" datetime="2026-04-07">Apr 2026</time><div class="moment-copy"><strong>The restricted-release moment</strong><p>Anthropic offered <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing">Claude Mythos Preview</a> only to selected cyber-defense partners and said that preview was not planned for general availability. It was not the first withheld model—the GPT-2 episode came years earlier—but it made model access itself a visible capability-dependent product decision.</p></div></div>
</div>
```

The [DeepSeek-R1 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) [@guo2025deepseekr1] documents the model family’s reinforcement-learning recipe and released distillations.

Together, these moments trace a progression: **conversation → tools → reasoning → agents → media → automatic orchestration → capability-dependent access**.

## The market follows the bottleneck

The clearest financial signal of the LLM era was Nvidia. Its GPUs became the scarce general-purpose compute behind both training and inference. Yet the AI trade did not remain a single “GPU stock” story: investor attention moved toward whichever hardware layer appeared scarce next. Use the event windows below to compare those price paths without confusing a quoted share price with company size.

```{=html}
<div data-ai-market-moments></div>
```

1. **GPU repricing.** On 25 May 2023, Nvidia shares [rose 24%](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/nvidia-close-to-becoming-first-trilliondollar-chip-firm-after-stellar-forecast-3090653) after an extraordinary data-center forecast. Its fiscal 2024 data-center revenue later reached $47.5 billion, up 217%, according to its [annual filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581024000029/nvda-20240128.htm).
2. **The DeepSeek shock.** [DeepSeek-R1 launched](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news250120/) on 20 January 2025. A week later, fear that more efficient models would require less hardware helped drive a [16.9% one-day Nvidia decline](https://apnews.com/article/52c54e361616509280bd2775674b6b4b). That was a change in investor expectations, not proof that compute demand had disappeared. Nvidia later recovered and [reached a $4 trillion market value](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/nvidia-becomes-first-company-to-clinch-4-trillion-in-market-value-4128409) in July 2025.
3. **The bottleneck expands.** AI systems need more than accelerators. High-bandwidth memory feeds model weights and activations to GPUs; [Micron said](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/micron-set-for-record-high-after-ai-demand-steers-strong-forecast-surprise-profit-3347470) its 2024 HBM capacity was sold out, and [SK hynix reported](https://news.skhynix.com/en/sk-hynix-announces-4q24-financial-results/) that HBM exceeded 40% of Q4 2024 DRAM revenue. CPUs coordinate storage, networking, retrieval, tool calls, and high-volume inference. By July 2026, [Intel reported](https://newsroom.intel.com/corporate/intel-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) stronger demand while [industry reporting](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/intel-sales-profit-forecast-beat-estimates-boosts-spending-plans-on-ai-boom-4809863) linked part of the CPU shortage to agentic workloads. These gains were specific to changing bottlenecks; they did not lift every hardware producer equally or prove that one workload single-handedly revived a company.

The economic lesson is that markets repeatedly try to identify the next scarce input. The technical lesson is similar: optimize the bottleneck that limits the whole system, not the component with the loudest story.

## Beyond text: VLMs, multimodality, and action

The output distinguishes several model interfaces. An **LLM** maps text tokens to text tokens, as in the dialogue examples earlier in the lecture. Vision-language, multimodal, and action models extend that interface in different directions.

### VLM: ground an image

A **vision-language model (VLM)** can connect a text instruction to visual evidence. In the example below, the input is a street photograph plus the instruction “Locate the bus and people.” The output grounds those words in regions of the image rather than returning only a sentence.

```{=html}
<figure class="model-example vision-grounding-example">
  <div class="vision-grounding-grid">
    <div class="vision-grounding-panel">
      <strong>Image input</strong>
      <img src="lecture-1/vlm-street-scene.jpg" alt="A city bus with several people walking in front of it on a street in Madrid.">
    </div>
    <div class="vision-grounding-panel">
      <strong>Grounded output</strong>
      <div class="vision-scene" role="img" aria-label="The same street photograph with one bounding box around the bus and three bounding boxes around people.">
        <img src="lecture-1/vlm-street-scene.jpg" alt="">
        <span class="vision-box vision-box--bus"><b>bus</b></span>
        <span class="vision-box vision-box--person-a"><b>person</b></span>
        <span class="vision-box vision-box--person-b"><b>person</b></span>
        <span class="vision-box vision-box--person-c"><b>person</b></span>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <figcaption>Illustrative grounding output on a real street photograph from the <a href="https://github.com/ultralytics/assets/blob/main/im/bus.jpg">Ultralytics example assets</a>. Bounding boxes make the connection between a word and an image region explicit.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

### Multimodal model: summarize a video

A multimodal model can combine evidence across time and return another medium. Here the input is a five-second video; the example output is a text summary of the full sequence.

```{=html}
<figure class="model-example multimodal-video-example">
  <div class="model-example-grid">
    <div>
      <strong class="model-example-label">Video input</strong>
      <video autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="auto" poster="lecture-1/multimodal-flower-poster.jpg" aria-label="A close-up time-lapse video of a red flower opening from a bud.">
        <source src="lecture-1/multimodal-flower.mp4" type="video/mp4">
        Your browser does not support embedded video.
      </video>
    </div>
    <div class="model-example-output">
      <strong>Text output</strong>
      <p>“A close-up time-lapse shows a red flower opening from a closed bud.”</p>
      <small>The change is visible only across the sequence: the first frame shows the bud, while later frames show the open flower.</small>
    </div>
  </div>
  <figcaption>Five-second CC0 sample video from <a href="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4">MDN Web Docs</a>. The clip autoplays muted and remains controllable.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

### VLA: turn perception into action

A **vision-language-action model (VLA)** extends the prediction target. Instead of ending with a sentence, the system must produce an action that changes the physical world:

$$
(\text{camera frames},\ \text{instruction},\ \text{robot state})
\longrightarrow
(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_T).
$$

```{=html}
<figure class="model-example vla-video-example">
  <div class="model-example-grid">
    <div>
      <strong class="model-example-label">Camera input and task</strong>
      <div class="video-embed">
        <iframe src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/7Q-FHj2r4NU?autoplay=1&amp;mute=1&amp;playsinline=1&amp;loop=1&amp;playlist=7Q-FHj2r4NU&amp;rel=0" title="Robohand autonomously throwing away trash" loading="lazy" allow="autoplay; encrypted-media; picture-in-picture; fullscreen" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="model-example-output">
      <strong>Action output</strong>
      <p>The system turns camera observations and the disposal task into a sequence of robot commands that moves the hand, grasps the trash, and discards it.</p>
      <small>Unlike a caption, the output changes the environment and must be evaluated for physical success and safety.</small>
    </div>
  </div>
  <figcaption><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Q-FHj2r4NU">Robohand finally throwing away the trash autonomously</a>, a hackathon demonstration by Alexan Hayrapetyan.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

[RT-2](https://deepmind.google/blog/rt-2-new-model-translates-vision-and-language-into-action/) [@zitkovich2023rt2] showed how web-scale vision-language knowledge could transfer into robotic control. [OpenVLA](https://github.com/openvla/openvla) [@kim2024openvla] later released a 7B open vision-language-action model trained on robot demonstrations. The promise is transfer: an instruction such as “move the can near the matching color” can draw on concepts learned outside a narrow robot dataset. The difficulty is that wrong physical actions have costs that wrong sentences do not.

### Specialization is another axis of progress

The same adaptation recipe used for Armenian can target a historical language such as Old English:

1. inspect whether the tokenizer fragments the language excessively;
2. assemble and document a clean, licensed corpus;
3. continue pre-training a suitable base model;
4. instruction-tune on translation, morphology, retrieval, or annotation tasks; and
5. evaluate on held-out texts with domain experts, not only with an automatic modern-language metric.

The research question is not “Can a giant model produce something that looks old?” It is whether the model preserves morphology, meaning, uncertainty, and source evidence on material it did not memorize. Recent [low-resource language-model research](https://aclanthology.org/2025.loreslm-1.21/) explores this continued-training route for historical languages.

## What to remember

1. **ChatGPT changed the interface more than the underlying definition of NLP.** Many tasks became instructions inside one dialogue system.
2. **RLHF learns preferences, not truth.** Demonstrations, rankings, a reward model, and policy optimization can improve behavior while introducing new failure modes.
3. **A benchmark score belongs to a protocol.** Checkpoint identity, prompts, tools, graders, and uncertainty matter as much as the headline number.
4. **The Llama 4 controversy was a reproducibility lesson.** An experimental chat variant and the public checkpoint were not interchangeable; that does not imply every result was fake.
5. **The model frontier is global but uneven.** The United States and China lead frontier-scale development, while regional ecosystems create value through sovereignty, deployment, openness, and language coverage.
6. **Capability shifts move engineering and economic bottlenecks.** Chat, reasoning, agents, native media, and routing changed how models were used, while demand moved across accelerators, memory, and infrastructure.
7. **Multimodal interfaces differ by their outputs.** VLMs can ground language in image regions, multimodal systems can interpret sequences such as video, and VLAs produce actions that change the physical world.
